1.title: Use Cases for AI and AWS AI Services
1.text: Welcome to Module two: Use Cases for A I and A W S A I Services. This module covers task statement one point two. You will learn where A I helps, where it does not, which technique fits which problem, and what each of the A W S A I services does. The exam gives you a need and asks you to name the technique or the service, so this module is about matching.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Recognize where A I and M L add value, and where they are not appropriate. Pick the right technique: classification, regression or clustering. Give real-world examples of A I applications. Explain what Transcribe, Translate, Comprehend, Lex, Polly, Rekognition, Textract, Personalize and SageMaker A I do. And decide when a traditional M L model or a foundation model fits.

1.title: Case Check-In: Cedar and Salt's AI Wish List
1.text: At Cedar and Salt Travel, the leaders write down six wishes. Turn call recordings into text. Translate listings. Find review sentiment. Read scanned invoices. Recommend trips. And build a booking chatbot. A seventh wish is a fixed fifteen percent group discount. Some wishes need A I, and one does not. Your job is to match each wish to the right technique or A W S service, and to spot the one that needs plain code.

1.title: Where AI and ML Add Value
1.text: Where does A I add value? First, it can assist human decision making, for example by ranking risky bookings so a person reviews the top few. Second, it can scale a solution, such as answering thousands of traveler questions at the same time. Third, it can automate repetitive work, like tagging photos, routing emails and extracting data from forms. It can also find patterns people cannot see in large amounts of data. A I usually supports people; it does not replace every decision. Exam tip: assist, scale and automate are the three classic reasons to use A I.

1.title: When AI Is Not Appropriate
1.text: The exam also asks when A I is not appropriate. One case is when a specific outcome is needed, not a prediction. Then use a rule or a formula, such as a fixed discount. Another is when the cost-benefit does not work, because the data, build and run costs exceed the value. A third is too little data, or poor-quality data. A fourth is when errors are costly and nobody can review them. And a fifth is when a simpler solution already does the job. Exam tip: if the answer is known and exact, write code instead of training a model.

1.title: Matching the Technique to the Problem
1.text: Now match the technique to the problem. Classification predicts a category. For example: will this booking be canceled, yes or no? Regression predicts a number. For example: what nightly price will fill the room? Clustering finds groups in unlabeled data. For example: which guest segments exist? Classification and regression use labeled data, so they are supervised, and clustering uses unlabeled data. Exam tip: a category means classification, a number means regression, and groups mean clustering.

1.title: Real-World AI Applications
1.text: Here are real-world A I applications, with examples at Cedar and Salt. Computer vision: checking listing photos for unsafe content. N L P: summarizing and classifying reviews. Speech recognition: transcribing support calls. Recommendation systems: trips you may like. Fraud detection: flagging suspicious payments. Forecasting: predicting demand by season. Knowledge bases: answering policy questions from company documents. And agentic A I: a booking agent that plans and acts. Exam tip: match the task to the field: see, read, listen, recommend, flag, predict, look up, or act.

1.title: Ready-Made Services, SageMaker AI or Foundation Models
1.text: There are three ways to get A I on A W S. The figure shows them as stacked cards. Ready-made A I services are called through an A P I, and they need no M L expertise; this module covers them. Amazon SageMaker A I lets you build, train and deploy your own models, and Module three covers it. Foundation models, through Amazon Bedrock, give you generative A I, and Modules four to seven cover them. Moving down the list gives more control and takes more effort. Exam tip: for a common task, when the team has no M L skills, start with a ready-made A I service.

1.title: Speech and Language: Transcribe, Translate and Polly
1.text: Three services handle speech and language. Amazon Transcribe is automatic speech recognition. It converts audio to text, in real time or from files in Amazon S three. Amazon Translate translates text between languages, on demand. Amazon Polly converts text into lifelike speech, with generative, neural and standard voices. You can chain them: Transcribe, then Translate, then Polly gives you spoken translation. Exam tip: audio in means Transcribe, text in another language means Translate, and speech out means Polly.

1.title: Text and Documents: Comprehend and Textract
1.text: Two services work on text and documents. Amazon Comprehend uses N L P to give you insights from text: entities, key phrases, language and sentiment, plus personal information and topics, and it can train custom classification. Think of it as meaning in text. Amazon Textract extracts printed and handwritten text, forms and tables from scanned documents and P D Fs. It also has queries, invoice and receipt analysis, and I D analysis. Think of it as data out of documents. Comprehend understands text that is already text, and Textract reads the scanned page first. Exam tip: sentiment or entities means Comprehend, and fields and tables from a scan mean Textract.

1.title: Images and Video: Amazon Rekognition
1.text: Amazon Rekognition is a deep learning image and video analysis service. It detects objects, scenes and text, and it detects unsafe content for moderation. It analyzes and compares faces, including face liveness checks. Custom Labels train a classifier for your own objects, such as logos. It needs no M L expertise: you call the A P I on files in Amazon S three. Exam tip: objects, faces and unsafe content in pictures or video mean Rekognition.

1.title: Conversation and Recommendations: Lex and Personalize
1.text: Two more services. Amazon Lex builds conversational interfaces for voice and text, with speech recognition and natural language understanding. Think of chatbots. Amazon Personalize is a fully managed service that makes item recommendations and user segments from your interaction data. Lex works with A W S Lambda to carry out the request. Personalize learns from clicks and purchases, not from the content of the items. Exam tip: a chatbot with voice or text means Lex, and people like you also booked means Personalize.

1.title: Amazon SageMaker AI: Your Own Models
1.text: When no ready-made service fits, use Amazon SageMaker A I. It is a fully managed M L service. Data scientists and developers use it to build, train and deploy M L models in a hosted environment. It supports built-in algorithms, your own algorithms and frameworks, and foundation models. Use it when you need something like a custom fraud model. A note on names: in December twenty twenty-four, Amazon SageMaker was renamed SageMaker A I, so older material uses the old name. Exam tip: a ready-made task means an A I service, and your own data and model mean SageMaker A I.

2.title: Traditional ML or a Foundation Model?
2.text: The guide also asks when a traditional M L model or a foundation model is appropriate. Structured, tabular prediction, such as cancellation or price, fits traditional M L. So does a regulatory need to explain each decision, because traditional models are more explainable. So does very high volume with tight cost and latency limits, because the models are smaller. Generating, summarizing or translating free text, and open-ended chat, fit a foundation model. So do many different language tasks with little labeled data, where you just prompt the model. Exam tip: explainable and structured means traditional M L, and open-ended language or content means a foundation model.

2.title: Service Chooser: I Need To...
2.text: Here is a chooser that starts from the need. I need to turn call recordings into text: Amazon Transcribe. Translate listings into other languages: Amazon Translate. Find the sentiment and entities in reviews: Amazon Comprehend. Pull fields and tables from scanned invoices: Amazon Textract. Flag unsafe content in photos: Amazon Rekognition. Read text out loud: Amazon Polly. Build a voice or text chatbot: Amazon Lex. Recommend trips to each traveler: Amazon Personalize. And train my own model: Amazon SageMaker A I. Exam tip: name the verb in the need, then the service.

2.title: What the Exam Asks: Use Cases and Services
2.text: Here is how the exam frames this module. Where it helps: assisting decisions, scaling and automating. Where it does not: exact rules, poor cost-benefit, little data and costly errors. Which technique: classification, regression or clustering. Which service: Transcribe, Translate, Comprehend, Textract, Rekognition, Polly, Lex, Personalize or SageMaker A I. And which model type: traditional M L for explainable, structured tasks, and a foundation model for open-ended language. Exam tip: read the verb in the question, then pick the service or technique.

2.title: Design Check: Cedar and Salt's Wish List
2.text: Now a design check. Cover the right column and answer each row yourself. Call recordings into text: Transcribe. Listings in many languages: Translate. Review sentiment: Comprehend. Scanned invoices into fields: Textract. Trip recommendations: Personalize. A booking chatbot: Lex. A fixed fifteen percent group discount: plain code, not A I. And a custom fraud model on its own data: SageMaker A I. Pause the video if you want more time.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Value: assist decisions, scale and automate. Not appropriate: an exact outcome, poor cost-benefit, little data and costly errors. Techniques: classification for categories, regression for numbers and clustering for groups. Services: Transcribe, Translate, Polly, Comprehend, Textract, Rekognition, Lex, Personalize and SageMaker A I. And for the model: traditional M L for explainable structured tasks, and a foundation model for open-ended language.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Cedar and Salt wants to turn recordings of customer support calls into text. Which A W S service should it use? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B, Amazon Transcribe. It is an automatic speech recognition service that converts audio to text. Polly does the reverse, Translate changes the language of text, and Comprehend analyzes text that already exists.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. The finance team receives scanned supplier invoices and wants the invoice numbers, dates and line-item tables as structured data. Which service fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A, Amazon Textract. It extracts printed and handwritten text, forms and tables from scanned documents, and it has an operation for invoices and receipts. Rekognition analyzes pictures, Polly makes speech, and Lex builds chatbots.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Select two. Which two of these are classification problems? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and D. Classification predicts a category, such as canceled or not, and fraudulent or legitimate. Estimating revenue or a price is regression, because it predicts a number, and grouping without labels is clustering.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Cedar and Salt's policy says every booking of ten or more guests gets exactly fifteen percent off. How should the team implement it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D, plain code, because the outcome is exact. When a specific outcome is required instead of a prediction, a rule or formula is the right tool. A model could produce a wrong discount, and the cost of building and running one is not justified.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Cedar and Salt wants to show each traveler trips they are likely to book, based on what they and similar travelers clicked and booked. Which service is built for this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C, Amazon Personalize. It generates item recommendations from interaction data such as clicks and purchases. Comprehend analyzes text, Rekognition analyzes images and video, and Translate translates text.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. The team wants a booking chatbot that understands typed and spoken requests and walks the traveler through a conversation. Which service should it use? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B, Amazon Lex. It builds conversational interfaces for voice and text, with speech recognition and natural language understanding. Polly only speaks, Transcribe only converts speech to text, and Textract reads documents.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. A lender must explain every credit decision to regulators, and its data is a structured table of customer attributes. Which approach fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D, a traditional M L model, which is easier to explain. Structured data and a regulatory need for explanations point to traditional M L. Foundation models are better for open-ended language and content, and the other options solve unrelated tasks.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all seven answers. Question one: B. Question two: A. Question three: A and D. Question four: D. Question five: C. Question six: B. Question seven: D. That completes Module two. Next, Module three covers the A I and M L lifecycle, M L operations, and the metrics that tell you whether a model is good.
